title: Women are reshaping publishing. That does not make books less intellectual.
subtitle: An online debate about books losing their intellectual status raises an older question: are we judging the writing, the business selling it—or the women who enjoy it?
author: ATHENA
body:
Original reporting date: 16 September 2026

Women’s growing presence in publishing is measurable. The suggestion that their presence makes literature less intellectually valuable is a different claim—and one that sales figures cannot establish.

In a 2023 research paper examining the US book market, economist Joel Waldfogel found that women had moved from publishing roughly a third as many books as men in 1970 to writing the majority of new books by 2020. His analysis drew on Amazon sales data and Goodreads ratings, and documented gains in readership and recognition for female-authored books. It described an expansion of creative participation, not a demonstrated decline in literary quality. The version reviewed here is a preliminary research paper, and its commercial and reader-rating measures are not a universal test of artistic merit.

The Book Leo’s April 2025 video, titled ‘soon books won’t be intellectual anymore…’, offers a starting point for examining the distinction. Three questions deserve separate answers: whether people are reading less, whether publishers are narrowing what they promote, and whether books associated with women receive a different kind of scrutiny.

Treating those questions as interchangeable turns women’s participation into an explanation before the evidence has been examined.

## The woman apologising for her novel is an old character

Jane Austen recognised the performance of literary embarrassment. In Chapter Five of Northanger Abbey, her narrator imagines a young woman responding to a question about her reading: ‘Oh! It is only a novel!’ She puts the book down with indifference or shame.

Austen then defends novels as works capable of displaying knowledge of human nature, wit and finely chosen language. The passage follows Catherine and Isabella spending time reading together: female companionship and pleasure become the occasion for an argument about intellectual value.

The point is not that every novel deserves admiration. It is that pleasure does not disqualify a work from serious attention. Nor does a female audience. A story about courtship can also be about inheritance, dependence, class and the limits of a woman’s choices.

![Portrait of Jane Austen by Cassandra Austen](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/91/JaneAusten%2C_by_Cassandra_Austen.jpg)

Portrait of Jane Austen in watercolour and pencil, circa 1810, by Cassandra Austen. Public domain. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:JaneAusten,_by_Cassandra_Austen.jpg Licence: https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/mark/1.0/

That distinction should guide contemporary criticism. A reviewer can demonstrate that a romance has thin characters, repetitive prose or an unconvincing resolution. Calling its readers unintelligent establishes none of those things. Equally, defending women’s reading does not require pretending every bestseller is formally daring or politically progressive.

## Follow the commercial decisions

There are legitimate questions about how books become visible. In a Publishers Association survey conducted by Savanta in October 2022, 59% of 2,001 UK respondents aged 16–25 said BookTok or book influencers had helped them discover a passion for reading. The poll was described as nationally representative, but it measured what respondents reported; it did not experimentally establish that TikTok caused a lasting change in reading habits.

The same release quoted independent bookseller Chrissy Ryan explaining that BookTok was influencing stocking decisions and demand forecasting. That is a concrete commercial mechanism: online recommendations can shape which books a shop expects to sell.

![A young woman reads in a bookstore](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/04/Taiwanese_young_woman_reading_in_the_bookstore.jpg)

Contextual photograph: a young woman reading in a Taiwanese bookstore, 29 September 2013. Photograph by BoChengChou. Source: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Taiwanese_young_woman_reading_in_the_bookstore.jpg Licence: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0/

The accountability question therefore belongs partly with businesses. How much space do publishers and retailers give unfamiliar voices, translations and books that are difficult to summarise in a short video? Do promotional budgets broaden discovery or repeatedly reinforce existing hits? These questions require evidence about acquisitions, marketing and shelf space—not assumptions about female readers’ intelligence.

The industry’s own figures resist a simple collapse narrative. In June 2026, the Publishers Association reported UK publishing revenue of £7.4 billion for 2025, including an 8% rise in fiction revenue. Chief executive Dan Conway welcomed growth across reading formats. Those are trade-body revenue figures spanning distinct markets; they neither prove that literary quality improved nor show that more individuals read books.

## Children’s reading needs attention, not a gender contest

The newer evidence also complicates claims of uninterrupted decline. The National Literacy Trust’s 2026 survey gathered responses from 125,375 children and young people aged 5–18 in 479 UK schools. Among 8–18-year-olds, 36.1% said they enjoyed reading in their free time, up from 32.7% in 2025. Daily reading rose from 18.7% to 20.3%.

The trust nevertheless warned that engagement remained low against the longer-term trend and that socioeconomic gaps had widened. These are reported attitudes and habits among surveyed pupils, not an intelligence test or evidence that women’s success in publishing causes boys to disengage.

Boys deserve books that interest them, access to libraries and adults who take their reading seriously. Girls deserve the same investment without being told that their enthusiasm has lowered the status of the activity. Neither goal requires narrowing whose stories count.

ATHENA’s standard should be demanding and consistent: examine what a book does with language, whose interior life it explores, which behaviour it rewards and what its ending asks readers to accept. Those questions apply to a bestselling romance as readily as to a prize-winning novel.

Women’s reading needs neither automatic celebration nor collective suspicion. It needs the respect of being discussed specifically. If a book is shallow, show where the writing fails. The gender of its audience is not the argument.
